justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what I infer was a baseline price around 107–108, likely for an equity index, commodity, or similar financial instrument. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed level, applying only a small expected drift since daily returns are typically near zero in expectation and mean reversion over very short windows is weak. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for slightly more drift, reflecting a mild bullish lean that could come from prevailing trend momentum or fundamental backdrop. At the one-month horizon, the point estimate rises further to 110, embodying a continued but modest upward trend assumption — roughly consistent with long-run average annualized equity returns scaled down to a monthly window.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized and implied volatility scaling with the square root of time, which is the standard statistical behavior for price uncertainty under random-walk assumptions. At one day, the interval is relatively tight (±3 points) because there is simply less time for prices to deviate. At one week, the interval widens to roughly ±6 points on each side, and at one month it expands to roughly ±13 points, reflecting accumulated uncertainty. Additional sources of uncertainty include liquidity conditions, the possibility of regime changes in volatility, and any scheduled macro events or earnings releases that could cause discontinuous jumps not fully captured by smooth volatility scaling.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include surprise central bank policy actions, geopolitical shocks, or a sudden deterioration in credit or liquidity conditions that triggers a sharp drawdown beyond the lower bound. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — such as a blowout economic data release, a major policy stimulus announcement, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could push prices well above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail events have more time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which underweight fat tails. In practice, financial returns exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a Gaussian model implies. This means the true probability of outcomes outside my stated 90% intervals is likely somewhat higher than the implied 10%, particularly in stressed market environments. Anyone using these forecasts should treat the outer bounds as soft rather than hard constraints.
